title: Mentally ill Geddes 'thrown in with the wolves' at Ottawa jail, inmate tells inquest
article: Cleve Geddes was drooling, disoriented and being taunted by other inmates the day before his suicide in the Ottawa jail where he had been "thrown in with the wolves," a fellow inmate told a coroner's inquest Tuesday.
Testifying by phone from Joyceville Institution, Jai Robert Middleton said he is still traumatized by what he saw happen to Geddes on B Pod at the Ottawa-Carleton Detention Centre on Feb. 7-8, 2017.

"He was dishevelled. He didn't know where he was. He was in really bad shape. He was shuffling his feet. He could barely talk. He just kept saying he shouldn't be there. He should be in hospital," Middleton said.

Geddes had been arrested the week before in Killaloe by OPP officers investigating a threats complaint made by Geddes' father. Geddes, a paranoid schizophrenic, had been ordered to hospital for a psychiatric assessment but ended up at the jail because no beds were available. He hanged himself in his cell on Feb. 8 and died two days later.
Middleton, who told the court he stood six-four and weighed 300 pounds, said Geddes approached him "because he felt safe around me."
"I really appreciated that he wasn't scared of me because of my size," Middleton told the inquest.

Geddes asked for help contacting a lawyer but couldn't get through because inmates can't call cellphones from the jail. Middleton helped Geddes reach a lawyer by having Middleton's wife connect a three-way call.
"Geddes wasn't scared. He was just sad he was there," said Middleton, who said he told other inmates to leave Geddes alone when he saw them making fun of him.
Middleton also said he told a guard that Geddes was ill and should be on the medical ward, but that "he just kind of brushed me off."

Middleton was watching from his cell when correctional officers found Geddes unconscious and unresponsive in his cell on Feb. 8. He heard the guards screaming and watched from his cell door window as paramedics frantically pumped on Geddes' chest.
"I knew he was gone," he said.

"I'm still dealing with a lot of stuff about his death. I'm also sitting here in tears thinking about him. I keep thinking about the family and how I tried to get in touch with somebody for him, whether it was lawyers or his mother or whoever it was - because he was calling them for help."

As Middleton spoke, Geddes's sisters, Sigrid and Bronwyn, held hands and stifled sobs from the gallery where they've sat throughout the six days of testimony. At times, Sigrid lay her head on Bronwyn's shoulder as they listened to Middleton's voice.

"It all comes together like a bad nightmare when I think about Mr. Geddes and how he didn't get help," Middleton said under cross-examination by Andrejs Berzins, who is representing MOMS, a support group for women whose loved ones are incarcerated.
He recommended the jail be more careful about where it houses vulnerable inmates.
"As it is, inmates with special needs are just thrown in with the wolves," he testified.

In other testimony, a deputy superintendent described changes that have occurred at the jail since Geddes' death. Francine Poulin said the jail has established a "step down unit" for inmates at risk where rules have been loosened and more counselling is available. Recreational officers are on hand to play games with inmates - ping pong is popular - and there is an interview room so psychologists don't have to conduct assessments through a slot in the cell door as they did for Geddes.
Poulin conceded, though, that the jail has a hard time recruiting and keeping psychologists on staff because of the low pay compared to the private sector.
The inquest, before presiding coroner Dr. Michael B. Wilson, is expected to end Friday with the jury's recommendations on how similar deaths might be prevented.
